Title: HoneyMyte Deploys CoolClient Backdoor with Kernel-Mode Rootkit

Victim.Description: Government entities in Myanmar, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Russia targeted by HoneyMyte.

diamond_model_summary: The HoneyMyte threat actor, also known as Mustang Panda, has been observed deploying the CoolClient backdoor with a kernel-mode rootkit. This operation targeted government entities in Myanmar, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Russia. The adversary used PlugX as an initial implant, followed by CoolClient for persistence and stealth. The kernel-mode rootkit enhances the malware's capabilities by hiding processes, files, and registry objects, making detection challenging. The infrastructure includes C2 communications facilitated through IOCTL requests. The victims are primarily government entities, indicating a high-severity espionage campaign.
doc_summary: The threat actor HoneyMyte, also known as Mustang Panda, has been observed deploying an updated version of the CoolClient backdoor with a signed Windows kernel-mode rootkit. This rootkit can hide and protect malicious processes, files, registry objects, and command-and-control (C2) network information. Kaspersky identified victims in Myanmar, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Russia, including government entities. CoolClient is deployed as a secondary backdoor following a PlugX infection. The kernel component is deployed when CoolClient has full access to the Service Control Manager and the SeTcbPrivilege privilege. If these conditions are not met, the malware skips driver deployment. Kaspersky published file hashes, paths, and C2 domains as indicators of compromise. The latest CoolClient variant can install the driver as a Windows service and control it from the user-mode backdoor through IOCTL requests. CoolClient supports keylogging, clipboard theft, credential harvesting, file management, and system reconnaissance. In one campaign targeting Myanmar, HoneyMyte used PlugX as the initial post-compromise implant to deploy CoolClient, adding Microsoft Defender exclusions for a fake Windows Defender installation directory and a renamed sideloading executable. The actor copied malware components into the directory, renamed a legitimate Sangfor executable to defender.exe for DLL sideloading, and established persistence through a scheduled task. Execution begins when the legitimate Sangfor application loads a malicious libngs.dll, which decrypts and executes the second-stage component loadcert.ini. The latter handles persistence, registry modifications, User Account Control (UAC) bypass, process injection, driver deployment, and loading the final-stage cert.ini implant responsible for C2 communications and backdoor functionality.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with the delivery of PlugX as an initial post-compromise implant, which then deploys the CoolClient backdoor. The installation phase involves setting up persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks and registry entries. The CoolClient backdoor communicates with C2 servers using IOCTL requests, allowing the adversary to maintain control over compromised systems. Actions on objectives include keylogging, credential harvesting, and system reconnaissance. The use of a kernel-mode rootkit enhances the malware's stealth capabilities, making detection and remediation more challenging.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes several indicators of compromise. Hash values and domain names are not explicitly mentioned, but the use of specific malware families like CoolClient and PlugX, along with the kernel-mode rootkit, are significant indicators. The rootkit's ability to hide processes and files, combined with the use of IOCTL requests for C2 communications, presents challenges for detection and response. The adversary's use of DLL sideloading and process injection techniques further complicates the detection process, requiring advanced monitoring and analysis tools.

doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified a large-scale phishing campaign named RecruitTrap, targeting marketing professionals through fake interview scheduling pages and Browser-in-the-Browser (BitB) windows. The campaign impersonates recruiters from over 50 organizations across 14 sectors, using more than 3,000 phishing URLs. It aims to steal Google and Facebook credentials and relay multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts in real time. The attack begins with unsolicited emails or meeting invitations, leading victims to counterfeit scheduling pages or recruitment portals. The phishing pages use a Svelte/SvelteKit front end and a persistent Socket.IO channel to control the victim's interaction. Most phishing pages use a Calendly theme and Cloudflare to hide the attackers' servers. The campaign is designed for rapid rebranding, targeting industries like recruitment, technology, luxury goods, and travel. Users are advised to verify interview invitations through official channels and organizations should use phishing-resistant authentication methods.
kill_chain_summary: The RecruitTrap campaign follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance through impersonation of recruiters, weaponization via fake scheduling pages, and delivery through phishing emails. Exploitation occurs when victims enter credentials on fake pages, followed by command and control using a persistent Socket.IO channel. The final stage involves actions on objectives, where stolen credentials are used to access corporate accounts.

The use of Cloudflare and AWS EC2 complicates detection, while the Browser-in-the-Browser technique and rapid rebranding increase the campaign's adaptability. Organizations should focus on detecting phishing domains and monitoring for unusual login attempts to mitigate the threat.

Title: Post-Exploitation Technique Using Chrome DevTools Protocol

Victim.Description: Windows systems running Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge are targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a post-exploitation technique using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to access cookies and authenticated sessions in Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge on Windows. The technique requires prior code execution and targets running browser processes. SpecterOps identified process injection activities detectable via Sysmon Event IDs 8 and 10. Google's updates to Chrome's remote debugging behavior aim to mitigate cookie theft risks. The CDP-Enable-BOF technique activates debugging from within a browser process, exposing context over a CDP port. The technique builds on prior work by DeathFlamingo and Cedric Van Bockhaven.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have detailed a post-exploitation technique involving the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) in Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge on Windows. This technique, requiring prior code execution, allows access to cookies and authenticated sessions. SpecterOps identified process injection targeting chrome.exe and msedge.exe, detectable via Sysmon Event IDs 8 and 10. Google updated Chrome's remote debugging behavior in version 136 to mitigate cookie theft. The CDP-Enable-BOF technique activates debugging from within a browser process, exposing context over a CDP port. The technique builds on prior work by DeathFlamingo and Cedric Van Bockhaven. SpecterOps' CDP-Toolkit enables interaction with the browser, preserving cookies and authentication states. Google's Device Bound Session Credentials in Chrome 146 aim to prevent cookie theft. The Hacker News confirmed the BOF's compatibility with specific Chrome and Edge versions. AmnesiaStealer targets macOS users, controlling Chromium browsers via CDP.
kill_chain_summary: The post-exploitation technique using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) involves several stages of the MITRE ATT&CK kill chain. During the exploitation stage, the technique leverages CDP for access to browser data. In the command and control stage, the CDP-Enable-BOF exposes the browser's context over a CDP port. The actions on objectives stage involves accessing cookies and authenticated sessions. Detection methods include monitoring Sysmon Event IDs 8 and 10 for process injection and unusual CDP network traffic. Remediation includes updating Chrome to version 136 or later and implementing Device Bound Session Credentials.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes several indicators. Tools such as CDP-Enable-BOF and CDP-Toolkit are used in the post-exploitation technique. Network host artifacts include process injection activities detectable via Sysmon Event IDs 8 and 10. The technique leverages the Chrome DevTools Protocol for command and control. No specific hash values, IP addresses, or domain names were identified. The Pyramid of Pain scoring reflects the presence of tools and network host artifacts, contributing to the overall assessment of the incident.

Title: Akira Ransomware Attack via SonicWall VPN Exploit

Victim.Description: The victim was targeted through a SonicWall VPN vulnerability.
Victim.Security_Posture: Compromised due to lack of MFA on VPN.

diamond_model_summary: The Akira ransomware attack involved an adversary exploiting a SonicWall VPN vulnerability to gain initial access. The adversary demonstrated capabilities in disabling endpoint detection and response solutions and exfiltrating data using tools like AnyDesk and WinRAR. The infrastructure involved compromised VPN access and cloud storage for data exfiltration. The victim's assets included domain controllers and application servers, with data types at risk being credentials and file shares. The attack's impact severity is high due to the potential for data extortion.
doc_summary: An Akira ransomware affiliate disabled the endpoint detection and response (EDR) solution on a compromised system by restarting the machine into Safe Mode with Networking. The attack occurred on August 4 after the hacker obtained initial access through an exposed SonicWall VPN device without multi-factor authentication (MFA). Managed detection and response (MDR) services company Huntress says that roughly two hours after a successful VPN login, the attacker connected to the domain controller via RDP, enumerated Active Directory users and computers, and then moved to an application server. They used WinRAR to archive mapped file shares and the command-line tool to upload the stolen data to an attacker-controlled S3 bucket, before installing AnyDesk for remote access. At that stage, the attacker used AnyDesk to force the compromised host to boot into Safe Mode with Networking and disable both the Huntress agent and Microsoft Defender’s real-time protection. Safe Mode is a Windows startup state designed for troubleshooting and diagnostic operations. It starts Windows with a limited set of drivers and services, generally preventing most third-party software and services from loading. For 10 minutes while in Safe Mode, the host had no working EDR, and AV was blinded. Meanwhile, the attackers added AnyDesk to Windows’ Safe Mode registry, allowing it to start after reboot and retain their remote access to the breached machine. However, when they attempted to launch the main ransomware payload (akira.exe) via AnyDesk in Safe Mode, it failed to execute as the system reported low virtual memory and generated out-of-memory and PowerShell errors. A scheduled Defender scan eventually detected the Akira executable, even if real-time protection was disabled in Safe Mode, but the security tool could not remove it while the machine remained in that mode. Defender quarantined the file only after the attacker rebooted the system into normal mode, which restored real-time protection. Despite the failure to encrypt files, the Akira operator still managed to steal credentials and files for data extortion, all in less than five hours from initial access. Huntress notes that other ransomware families, such as Snatch and AvosLocker, have used this tactic for years, but this incident marks the first time the company observed it in an Akira attack. The researchers recommend adding MFA to all VPN accounts, placing credential-spraying detection measures, and monitoring for Safe Mode boot configuration changes or remote-access tools being added to the Safe Mode service registry.
kill_chain_summary: The attack followed a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance to identify the exposed SonicWall VPN. Initial access was gained through exploiting the VPN vulnerability, followed by lateral movement using RDP. The adversary installed AnyDesk for persistence and used it for command and control. Actions on objectives included attempted ransomware execution and data exfiltration. Defensive evasion was achieved by disabling EDR and AV in Safe Mode. The attack highlights the importance of MFA and monitoring for unauthorized access.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes tools like AnyDesk and WinRAR, which are relatively easy for adversaries to replace. The use of specific techniques such as disabling EDR in Safe Mode and exploiting VPN vulnerabilities are more challenging for adversaries to change. The incident underscores the need for robust detection and response capabilities to address these higher-level indicators of compromise.

diamond_model_summary: The AmnesiaStealer incident involves a sophisticated adversary using a Rust-based infostealer to target macOS users. The adversary employs phishing techniques via a counterfeit GitHub page to deliver the malware. The capability includes browser session hijacking and credential harvesting. The infrastructure relies on a remote server for payload delivery and control. Victims are macOS users globally, with a focus on harvesting credentials and session data.
doc_summary: AmnesiaStealer is a Rust-based information stealer targeting macOS users, capable of hijacking Chromium web browsers to steal session data. It spreads via a counterfeit GitHub download page using a ClickFix-style lure. The attack chain involves a multi-stage deployment, starting with a shell script that downloads the payload, followed by a Rust infostealer that harvests data from Keychain, browsers, Apple Notes, and Telegram. The final stage involves a stream_module for remote control of the victim's browser. The stealer captures system passwords and uses them for privileged access, storing them in cleartext. It targets various file types and uses a stealth script to evade detection. The malware's objectives align with other stealers like Atomic Stealer, but it features a builder-driven configuration and a remote-control second stage.
kill_chain_summary: The AmnesiaStealer attack follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance through a counterfeit GitHub page. Weaponization involves creating a Rust-based infostealer. Delivery is achieved via phishing, leading to exploitation through user execution of a Base64-encoded command. Installation involves deploying the infostealer and dropper script. Command and control are established via WebSocket connections, allowing remote control. Actions on objectives include harvesting credentials and session data.

doc_summary: APT36, also known as Transparent Tribe, is conducting a cyber campaign targeting Afghan telecom providers and South Asian critical infrastructure. The campaign involves the deployment of a new backdoor called PATCHCORD, delivered via fake VPN installers impersonating Afghan Telecom. Another backdoor, SHEETCORD, uses Google Sheets for command-and-control communications and targets Indian government IT networks. The campaign infrastructure includes a single C2 server with multiple associated domains, including those impersonating Afghan telecom operators and a hijacked healthcare domain. The threat actor's tactics include browser shortcut hijacking, remote command execution via PowerShell, and persistence mechanisms using the Windows Registry and Startup folder. The campaign reflects an evolution in APT36's operations, with a focus on Afghan telecom providers and Indian government, defense, and energy sectors. The use of AI-assisted malware projects like HACKERAI C2 and open-source C2 frameworks indicates a sophisticated offensive toolkit.

The group weaponizes malware like PATCHCORD and SHEETCORD, delivering them via fake VPN installers and impersonated domains. Command and control is achieved using Google Sheets and GitHub Gists, enabling espionage activities targeting sensitive data.

diamond_model_summary: The WindRelay and SpyNote incident showcases a sophisticated adversary using a combination of social engineering, RAT, and NFC relay malware to conduct financial fraud. The adversary's capability includes exploiting Android devices to capture NFC data and control devices remotely. The infrastructure involves a shared C2 over WebSocket for real-time data relay. doc_summary: WindRelay is a newly identified Android NFC relay malware family used in conjunction with the SpyNote RAT for contactless payment fraud. Detected in August 2025, it captures live card data via NFC, transmitting it to fraudsters. The malware exploits SpyNote's Accessibility Service to sideload the NFC app silently. Victims are lured through phishing, smishing, or vishing to install the malicious app, which then turns their device into a payment proxy. The malware has spread from the Czech Republic to Brazil, Poland, and Slovakia. Group-IB highlights its dual monetization strategy, enabling digital loans and card-present purchases. ESET notes the potential for large-scale automated fraudulent transactions. The malware uses WebSocket for C2 communication, relaying EMV APDU commands. VirusTotal has 23 samples impersonating financial institutions in Czechia, Slovakia, and Slovenia.
kill_chain_summary: The WindRelay and SpyNote attack follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to gather victim details for personalized attacks. Weaponization involves creating a personalized APK file. Delivery is achieved through phishing, smishing, or vishing. Exploitation occurs via SpyNote's Accessibility Service to sideload the NFC app. Installation of the NFC relay malware follows, maintaining persistence on the victim's device. Command and control is established using WebSocket for real-time data relay. Finally, actions on objectives involve conducting financial fraud using the NFC relay malware.

doc_summary: Threat actors are exploiting a critical Microsoft SharePoint vulnerability, CVE-2026-55040, with a CVSS score of 9.1. This vulnerability allows attackers to bypass authentication due to weak JWT token validation, enabling them to impersonate SharePoint users. The PoC exploit was released by Rapid7, leading to 12 recorded exploitation attempts from eight unique IP addresses across five countries: Hong Kong, Japan, Netherlands, Taiwan, and the United States. Microsoft patched this vulnerability in July 2026. The exploitation involves chaining four weaknesses to forge a valid JWT token, allowing attackers to perform arbitrary operations on SharePoint servers. Telemetry data from KEVIntel shows a spike in exploitation attempts, particularly on August 12 and 13, 2026. SharePoint users are advised to update their systems to mitigate this threat.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a campaign using malicious browser extensions to impersonate well-known VPN services. The adversary's infrastructure includes SOCKS5 proxies and a shared analytics account, targeting Russian users. doc_summary: A campaign involving over 737 malicious browser extensions on the Chrome Web Store impersonated well-known VPN and proxy services, such as Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver. These extensions routed user traffic through SOCKS5 proxies operated by a single provider, primarily targeting Russian users seeking to bypass blocked services. The campaign utilized 40 publisher accounts and a shared analytics account, resulting in nearly 75,000 downloads. The threat actor's server could intercept all browser traffic, including destination, TLS SNI values, source IP, and plain HTTP request bodies. Despite Google removing over 200 extensions, more than 500 remain available. Socket researchers identified indicators of deception, suggesting the campaign aimed to funnel users to a subscription-based VPN service in Russia.
kill_chain_summary: The attack follows a structured kill chain: reconnaissance to identify popular VPN services, weaponization through the creation of malicious extensions, delivery via the Chrome Web Store, installation by users, and command and control through SOCKS5 proxies. The adversary's actions on objectives include potential data collection and traffic monitoring.

Title: Lazarus Group Exploits Zero-Day in Windows for Espionage Campaign

Victim.Description: Targeted defense and aerospace companies in multiple countries.

diamond_model_summary: The Lazarus Group, a North Korean state-sponsored actor, executed a sophisticated cyber espionage campaign targeting defense and aerospace sectors in France, Germany, Brazil, and India. The group exploited a zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Windows (CVE-2026-68820) to deploy a backdoor named Troy. The campaign, part of Operation Dream Job, used social engineering tactics, including fake job offers on LinkedIn, to lure victims. The attackers employed a kernel-mode rootkit for persistence and hijacked legitimate infrastructure for command and control, complicating detection efforts.
doc_summary: The North Korean threat actor Lazarus Group has been linked to exploiting a zero-day vulnerability, CVE-2026-68820, in Microsoft Windows to deploy a backdoor named Troy targeting defense and aerospace sectors in France, Germany, Brazil, and India. This activity is part of Operation Dream Job, a campaign using social engineering tactics to lure professionals with fake job offers. The attack chain involves exploiting a privilege escalation flaw in AFD.sys, installing a kernel-mode rootkit, and using compromised infrastructure for command and control. The campaign also involves phishing tactics using fake recruiter profiles on LinkedIn and impersonating legitimate companies like Enveil. The attackers have hijacked legitimate WordPress and SharePoint sites for C2 operations, making detection challenging. The campaign highlights the sophistication of Lazarus Group in blending legitimate infrastructure with malicious activities.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance to identify targets in the defense and aerospace sectors. Weaponization involved creating malicious PDFs and trojanized PDF viewers. Delivery was achieved through phishing emails. Exploitation of CVE-2026-68820 allowed privilege escalation. Installation involved deploying the Troy backdoor and a kernel-mode rootkit. Command and control were maintained using compromised infrastructure. Finally, actions on objectives included exfiltrating sensitive data. The campaign's sophistication is evident in its use of zero-day vulnerabilities and legitimate infrastructure for C2 operations.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes several challenging indicators. The use of a zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-68820) and sophisticated malware like the Troy backdoor and kernel-mode rootkit represent high-level TTPs. The hijacking of legitimate infrastructure for command and control adds complexity to detection efforts. The campaign's reliance on social engineering tactics, such as fake job offers on LinkedIn, further complicates attribution and response. Overall, the incident demonstrates the Lazarus Group's advanced capabilities and persistence in achieving its espionage objectives.

Title: Operation Dream Job: Exploitation of Windows Zero-Day by Lazarus Group

Victim.Description: The campaign targets defense, aerospace, and aviation organizations, particularly those involved in military technologies.
Victim.Security_Posture: Targeted organizations may have varying levels of security maturity.

diamond_model_summary: The Lazarus Group, a North Korean state-sponsored actor, targeted defense-sector companies using a Windows zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-68820) in the Operation Dream Job campaign. The group employed sophisticated malware, including the FudModule rootkit and Troy backdoor, to gain SYSTEM privileges and exfiltrate sensitive information. The campaign had a global reach, affecting organizations in Europe, India, and South America.
doc_summary: North Korean hackers, identified as the Lazarus Group, have been exploiting a Windows zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-68820) in the Operation Dream Job campaign. This campaign targets defense-sector companies, particularly in Europe and India, using fraudulent recruitment offers. The vulnerability is a use-after-free in Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock (AFD.sys), allowing attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges. The Lazarus Group has incorporated an exploit for CVE-2026-68820 into a new version of the FudModule kernel-mode rootkit, which disables EDR telemetry and interferes with security products. Additionally, a new backdoor called Troy, supporting 17 commands, has been deployed. The campaign has a global reach, with activity in South America and successful targeting in Western Europe. Check Point researchers observed scans targeting vulnerable Roundcube installations, compromised with a PHP web shell dubbed RelayShell. The attackers likely used leaked credentials to authenticate to Roundcube before exploiting an authenticated PHP object-deserialization vulnerability for remote code execution.
kill_chain_summary: The attack followed a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance to identify targets in the defense sector. The Lazarus Group weaponized the CVE-2026-68820 vulnerability and delivered malware via spear-phishing emails. Exploitation of the vulnerability allowed the installation of the FudModule rootkit and Troy backdoor, enabling command and control through compromised Roundcube instances. The attackers aimed to exfiltrate sensitive military information.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes various indicators such as the FudModule rootkit and Troy backdoor (Tools), CVE-2026-68820 (TTPs), and compromised Roundcube instances (Network Host Artifacts). These indicators provide opportunities for detection and response, with the potential to disrupt the attacker's operations by identifying and mitigating these elements.

doc_summary: A large-scale cyber incident involving 737 VPN and proxy extensions targeting Russian-speaking users was discovered. These extensions, found on the Chrome Web Store, impersonate 66 established VPN brands like Proton VPN and NordVPN. They route browser traffic through a SOCKS5 proxy, placing the threat actor in an adversary-in-the-middle position. The extensions have been installed 75,486 times, with 221 removed from the store. The threat actor is linked to a VPN business in Russia, using a 12-digit taxpayer number. The extensions bypass only loopback addresses, funneling all other traffic through the proxy. The incident highlights the risks of browser extensions and the potential for data interception.

Title: Flaw in AI Reasoning APIs Exposes Sensitive Data

Victim.Description: The victims were users of AI reasoning APIs who had their sensitive data exposed through reasoning block replay attacks.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involved a vulnerability in AI reasoning APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, allowing researchers to extract sensitive data from encrypted reasoning blocks. The attack did not require encryption keys but relied on replaying reasoning blocks across sessions and models. The exposure was limited to users who published raw agent logs with reasoning objects intact.
doc_summary: A newly disclosed flaw in AI reasoning APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google allowed researchers to extract internal reasoning and secrets from session logs. The vulnerability affected encrypted reasoning objects, enabling cross-user attacks to recover sensitive data such as API keys and passwords. The attack did not require encryption keys but relied on replaying reasoning blocks across sessions and models. The researchers demonstrated four abuse paths, including model distillation and prompt injection. The issue was disclosed to Microsoft and Hugging Face, with mitigations reportedly stopping the attacks. The study highlights the need for developers to strip reasoning blocks from shared traces to prevent exposure.
kill_chain_summary: The attack exploited a flaw in AI reasoning APIs to extract sensitive data, such as API keys and passwords, from encrypted reasoning blocks. The exploitation stage involved replaying reasoning blocks across sessions and models, while the actions on objectives stage included unauthorized actions like model distillation and prompt injection. Mitigations reportedly stopped the attacks.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain analysis reveals that no specific indicators such as hashes, IPs, or domains were identified. The attack relied on exploiting a flaw in AI reasoning APIs, making it challenging to detect using traditional indicators. The focus should be on securing reasoning blocks and preventing their replay across sessions and models.

Title: Sandworm's Social Engineering Campaign Targeting IT Professionals

Victim.Description: The victims are system administrators and IT professionals targeted through fake job offers.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves the Russian threat group Sandworm, specifically sub-cluster UAC-0145, targeting IT professionals through social engineering. The adversary uses trojanized software to gain access to corporate networks. The infrastructure includes fake domains and modified software hosted on SourceForge. Victims are system administrators and IT professionals in the Information Technology sector, primarily in Ukraine.
doc_summary: Hackers associated with the Russian threat group Sandworm, specifically sub-cluster UAC-0145, have been targeting system administrators and IT professionals through fake job offers since at least May. The Ukrainian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-UA) reported this social engineering campaign, where attackers pose as IT companies and recruiters. They study resumes on job sites and contact victims directly, moving conversations to Telegram and arranging video interviews over Zoom. During these interviews, candidates receive mock technical assignments requiring connection to a corporate VPN. In one observed case, attackers impersonated Sopra Steria using legitimate-looking email addresses. Instructions for the technical interview included configuration files for connecting to a 'corporate' VPN using WireGuard. The downloaded file produces a fake error, prompting victims to download a modified WireGuard client called 'SopraVPN' from SourceForge. This trojanized client supports a malicious 'SymmetricKey' configuration option that decrypts and executes embedded PowerShell code. On Windows, it creates a scheduled task and downloads an additional payload. On Linux, it uses cURL to retrieve another executable. CERT-UA advises telecommunications providers and IT companies to restrict access to managed, monitored devices protected by EDR.
kill_chain_summary: The attack follows a structured kill chain: reconnaissance through resume analysis, weaponization via trojanized software, delivery through email and SourceForge, exploitation by executing the trojanized client, installation of persistence mechanisms, command and control via modified VPN clients, and actions on objectives by downloading additional payloads. Each stage involves specific tactics and techniques, with detection and remediation strategies recommended.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names like sourceforge.net, tools such as SopraVPN and WireGuard, and TTPs involving social engineering and trojanized software. These indicators are crucial for detection and response efforts. The adversary's use of custom Base64 decoding and PowerShell scripts adds complexity to the analysis, requiring advanced detection capabilities.

The infrastructure is designed to be robust against takedown efforts, and the botnet targets Android TV boxes and Linux IoT devices. The victim profile includes consumer electronics, specifically devices with ADB enabled, which are vulnerable to exploitation. The adversary's strategic objectives include maintaining operational resilience and conducting impactful DDoS attacks.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 discovered a new version of the Kimwolf/AISURU botnet, known as Kimwolf v7, in February 2026. This botnet targets Android and IoT devices, particularly Android TV boxes with ADB enabled on port 5555. Kimwolf v7 introduces an HTTP/2-based DDoS flood that constructs complete browser fingerprints, making attack traffic harder to distinguish from legitimate browsing. The botnet's command-and-control infrastructure is enhanced with Ethereum Name Service (ENS), a Tor .onion hidden service, and a local proxy for routing between clearnet and Tor. The botnet has removed scanning and exploitation functionalities, indicating a separation of the propagation pipeline from the core payload. Kimwolf operators distribute Android APK packages masquerading as SystemService, probing for root access and executing ELF kernel payloads. The botnet has been active since mid-2024, with significant operational security adjustments observed in late 2025.
kill_chain_summary: The Kimwolf v7 botnet follows a structured kill chain, beginning with the weaponization of malware with DDoS capabilities and resilient C2 infrastructure. Delivery occurs via ADB on Android TV boxes, exploiting vulnerabilities such as Dirty COW for privilege escalation. Installation involves masquerading as system processes to maintain persistence. Command and control are achieved through encrypted channels using ENS and Tor, ensuring resilient communication. The final stage, actions on objectives, involves conducting DDoS attacks using HTTP/2 floods, impacting targeted systems and networks.

doc_summary: Cisco has identified a high-severity denial-of-service vulnerability, CVE-2026-20349, in its Secure Firewall ASA and Threat Defense (FTD) software. This vulnerability, with a severity score of 8.6, is actively exploited to remotely crash affected devices. It impacts devices running Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) or Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software with certain remote access services enabled. The flaw is due to insufficient error checking while processing HTTP requests. Exploitation can occur remotely without authentication when SSL listen sockets are enabled. Vulnerable configurations include IKEv2 Remote Access VPN with client services, SSL VPN, and Zero Trust Network Access on FTD devices. Cisco has released hot fixes for affected ASA and FTD releases. No workarounds exist, and Cisco recommends upgrading to a fixed software release. The vulnerability was discovered during Cisco's internal security testing and independently reported by security researcher Valerio Brussani.

The capability involves exploiting a deserialization of untrusted data weakness, allowing arbitrary code execution. The infrastructure includes exposed SharePoint servers, primarily affecting government agencies in the United States. The victim profile includes Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies, with a high impact severity due to the potential compromise of sensitive organizational data.
doc_summary: CISA confirmed that ransomware gangs are exploiting a high-severity Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-45659, which has been actively exploited since early July. This vulnerability arises from a deserialization of untrusted data weakness, allowing attackers with low privileges to execute arbitrary code on unpatched SharePoint servers. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure their servers within three days. CISA also urged security teams to monitor affected servers for signs of exploitation, apply Microsoft's latest patches, verify successful installation, and shorten patching cycles. Shadowserver tracks exposed online SharePoint servers, with many unpatched against CVE-2026-45659. Microsoft has yet to update the CVE-2026-45659 advisory to tag it as exploited.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain for this incident primarily involves the exploitation stage, where ransomware gangs exploit the CVE-2026-45659 vulnerability in Microsoft SharePoint servers. The adversaries gain initial access through this remote code execution vulnerability, which does not require significant prior knowledge of the system. The exploitation is facilitated by the deserialization of untrusted data weakness, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code with low privileges. Detection involves monitoring SharePoint server logs for unusual activity and checking for signs of exploitation. Remediation includes applying Microsoft's latest patches and enabling Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) integration.

doc_summary: The GhostSplice technique, disclosed by ASSET Research Group, targets AI coding assistants using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A malicious MCP server fragments requests to exfiltrate SSH keys, environment secrets, source code, and customer data. The attack exploits coding tools connected to external servers, bypassing safety controls. GhostSplice assumes prior connection to the attacker's server and access to files. The technique's effectiveness varies across models, with compliance rates increasing when requests are split. ASSET's tests show vulnerabilities in AI models like GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Llama 3.3 70B. The attack highlights the importance of client-side defenses and treating server output as data, not instructions. GhostSplice follows Ghostcommit, another ASSET disclosure, emphasizing the need for robust safety boundaries around AI models.
kill_chain_summary: The GhostSplice attack follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable AI coding assistants. Weaponization involves preparing fragmented requests, followed by delivery via the MCP protocol. The attack underscores the importance of securing AI environments and monitoring MCP traffic.

Title: Abuse of Windows Plug and Play for SYSTEM Access via Emulated USB Devices

Victim.Description: Targets Windows 11 systems with enabled Plug and Play or USB redirection.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves adversaries exploiting Windows Plug and Play vulnerabilities to gain SYSTEM access on Windows 11 machines. The capability includes emulating USB devices to trigger the installation of privileged software components. The infrastructure leverages Remote Desktop Protocol for remote exploitation. Victims are Windows 11 systems with enabled Plug and Play or USB redirection.
doc_summary: Security researchers Alejandro Hernando and Borja Martinez demonstrated a technique to exploit Windows Plug and Play (PnP) to gain SYSTEM access on a fully updated Windows 11 machine. The attack involves emulating USB devices to trigger the installation of signed vendor software, which can be abused for privilege escalation. The researchers presented their findings at DEF CON 34, detailing how an unprivileged user can leverage the PnP installation path for SYSTEM code execution. The attack chain includes emulating a Sierra Wireless device to install SwiService.exe, exploiting a SetDNS primitive, and using a Sony FeliCa reader to place a DLL in System32 via a path-traversal flaw. The remote variant uses synthetic USB traffic over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) to achieve similar results. Microsoft notes that USB redirection is not enabled by default, and administrators can restrict device installations by hardware ID. The research highlights vulnerabilities in legitimate installation paths and third-party packages, emphasizing the need for careful configuration and monitoring.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with the weaponization of tools to emulate USB devices, followed by delivery through emulation to trigger PnP installation. Exploitation occurs via PnP vulnerabilities, leading to the installation of malicious components. The final stage involves achieving SYSTEM access through path traversal and search-order hijacking.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes tools for USB emulation and TTPs such as path traversal and search-order hijacking. No specific hash values, IP addresses, or domain names were identified. The focus is on exploiting legitimate installation paths and vulnerabilities in third-party packages.

Title: Supply Chain Compromise of BdThemes WordPress Plugins

Victim.Description: WordPress sites using BdThemes plugins were targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The supply chain compromise of BdThemes WordPress plugins involved adversaries exploiting a cross-site scripting vulnerability to execute scripts in admin browsers. The attack was API-driven, requiring no plugin updates, and aimed to establish covert administrative persistence and remote code execution.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers identified a supply chain compromise affecting BdThemes WordPress plugins. The attack involved poisoning a static remote JSON data stream used by an administrative promotional banner component, exploiting a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw in the JSON response parsing code. The vulnerability, rated medium severity, allowed attackers to inject scripts that executed in the browser of logged-in administrators, creating rogue admin accounts and uploading web shell plugins. The attack was API-driven, requiring no plugin updates or file modifications. The C2 server used in this campaign is linked to other supply chain attacks, indicating a goal of establishing covert administrative persistence and remote code execution across WordPress environments.
kill_chain_summary: The attack followed a structured kill chain: reconnaissance to identify vulnerable plugins, weaponization of JSON payloads, delivery via API, exploitation of XSS vulnerability, installation of rogue admin accounts, command and control communication with a C2 server, and actions on objectives to maintain persistence.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes tools like JavaScript payloads (w2.js, x.js) and TTPs such as supply chain compromise and cross-site scripting. The attack leveraged API-driven delivery and C2 communication, making detection and remediation challenging.

Title: Cyberattack on Polish CHP Plant via Private APN

Victim.Description: A Polish combined heat and power plant serving approximately 50,000 residents.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to default credentials and lack of network segmentation.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involved an unknown adversary exploiting network vulnerabilities and default credentials to disrupt operations at a Polish CHP plant. The adversary used SSH tunneling and leveraged existing device functions to achieve their objectives. The infrastructure included a private APN and compromised network devices, while the victim was a critical energy sector facility in Poland.
doc_summary: In December 2025, attackers infiltrated a Polish combined heat and power plant, disrupting operations by exploiting a private APN used by the local grid operator. The attack began at a wind farm with a compromised FortiGate device, allowing access to the plant's network. The attackers used SSH tunneling through a Teltonika RUTX50 router to reach a WAGO PFC200 controller with default admin credentials. They connected to Siemens PLCs over the S7 protocol, switching them to STOP mode, which shut down the turbine and process-water treatment system. CERT Polska investigated the incident, noting the use of default credentials and lack of multi-factor authentication as key vulnerabilities. The attack did not involve malware but leveraged existing device functions and protocols. The incident highlights the risks of private APN configurations and the need for improved security measures in industrial networks.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance activities, including scanning the APN for vulnerable devices. The adversary then exploited default credentials to gain access to the network, using SSH tunneling for command and control. Actions on objectives involved switching Siemens PLCs to STOP mode, disrupting operations. The attack did not involve malware but relied on existing device functions and protocols.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and network host artifacts, such as the use of default credentials and SSH tunneling. These indicators are moderately difficult for adversaries to change, making them valuable for detection and response efforts. The incident highlights the importance of securing network configurations and enforcing strong authentication measures.

Title: Cyberattack on Polish CHP Plant via Private APN

Victim.Description: The victim was a small CHP plant in Poland's energy sector.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involved the Electrum threat group targeting a Polish CHP plant. The adversary exploited a misconfigured private APN to gain access to the operational technology network. They used default credentials on a WAGO PLC to further infiltrate the network, demonstrating high sophistication and a strategic objective to disrupt energy operations.
doc_summary: In December 2025, a cyberattack targeted Poland's energy sector, specifically a small combined heat-and-power (CHP) plant. The attack was linked to the Russian Electrum threat group. The attacker exploited a misconfigured private Access Point Name (APN) network, initially compromising a FortiGate VPN/firewall at a wind farm. They used a Teltonika cellular router to tunnel into the APN, which lacked client isolation, allowing lateral movement. The attacker accessed a WAGO PFC200 PLC with default credentials, enabling SSH to bridge into the plant's operational technology (OT) network. They scanned for SCADA systems and Siemens PLCs, eventually shutting down the steam turbine and water treatment system. The attack was short-lived, with no impact on the population. The Polish CERT highlighted this as the first known real-world cyberattack using a private APN for OT network access.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance through network scanning, followed by exploitation of default credentials on a WAGO PLC. The adversary used SSH for command and control, ultimately achieving their objective by disabling critical systems. The attack highlighted vulnerabilities in private APN configurations and the need for improved network security measures.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The attack utilized specific tools and techniques, including the exploitation of default credentials and SSH for command and control. The lack of specific indicators such as hashes or IP addresses limits the ability to apply the Pyramid of Pain effectively. However, the incident underscores the importance of securing network configurations and monitoring for unauthorized access.

Title: Storm-1175 Deploys New Ransomware StormEncryptor

Victim.Description: Victims are likely organizations using vulnerable versions of N-able N-central.

diamond_model_summary: Storm-1175, a financially motivated threat actor from China, has shifted tactics by deploying a new ransomware strain, StormEncryptor. This group is known for exploiting vulnerabilities in various software to gain initial access. Their infrastructure involves exploiting internet-facing systems, and they have a history of rapid ransomware deployment. Victims are likely organizations using vulnerable software, with a high impact severity due to the potential for data exfiltration and system compromise.
doc_summary: Microsoft disclosed that Storm-1175, a financially motivated threat actor linked to China, deployed a new ransomware strain called StormEncryptor. This marks a shift from their previous use of Medusa ransomware. StormEncryptor is written in C++ and appends the .encrypted extension to files. It drops a ransom note named !!!README_FIRST!!!.txt. The campaign likely exploits CVE-2026-18577, a security flaw in N-able N-central, for initial access. This vulnerability is a patch bypass for CVE-2026-18556, allowing authentication bypass and account takeover. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) flagged these vulnerabilities as actively exploited. Storm-1175 has a history of exploiting vulnerabilities in Mirth Connect, ConnectWise ScreenConnect, JetBrains TeamCity, and Fortinet FortiClient EMS. They weaponize zero-days and N-day vulnerabilities for high-velocity attacks. Post-compromise, they use AnyDesk, SimpleHelp, Advanced IP Scanner, and Mimikatz. Rapid movement from initial access to data exfiltration and ransomware deployment is observed.
kill_chain_summary: The attack by Storm-1175 follows a structured kill chain, beginning with the exploitation of a vulnerability (CVE-2026-18577) in N-able N-central for initial access. The installation phase involves deploying the StormEncryptor ransomware, which appends the .encrypted extension to files. Command and control are maintained using remote access tools like AnyDesk and SimpleHelp. The final stage involves data exfiltration and ransomware deployment, emphasizing the need for rapid patching and monitoring.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes several key indicators. The use of specific tools like AnyDesk and SimpleHelp, along with the deployment of StormEncryptor ransomware, provides actionable intelligence. The exploitation of CVE-2026-18577 and related vulnerabilities highlights the importance of timely patching. Monitoring for the creation of files with the .encrypted extension and unusual remote access tool usage can aid in detection and response efforts.

doc_summary: Justin Swaddle, a member of 'The Com', a cybercrime collective targeting children and teenagers, was sentenced to two years in prison for blackmail and sextortion offenses against nearly 120 victims worldwide. diamond_model_summary: The incident involves threat actors using AI to enhance traditional identity attacks. They leverage AI to automate and personalize phishing and credential theft, exploiting leaked credentials from breaches. The infrastructure includes rotating IP addresses and disposable browser profiles to mimic legitimate logins. Victims are organizations relying on traditional identity security methods, facing high impact severity due to AI-enhanced attacks.
doc_summary: Identity security is increasingly challenged by AI-enhanced attacks. Traditional methods like passwords, MFA, IP reputation, and geolocation are becoming less effective as attackers use AI to automate and personalize phishing, credential theft, and social engineering. Attackers exploit leaked credentials from breaches, bypass MFA through phishing and adversary-in-the-middle attacks, and use residential proxies to mask malicious logins. Zero Trust measures and device trust are crucial to counter these threats. Organizations must scan for leaked credentials and adapt security policies to account for device health and compliance. AI reduces the manual effort in attacks, allowing threat actors to focus on high-value targets.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves reconnaissance through gathering public information, weaponization by creating AI-personalized phishing emails, delivery via phishing emails, exploitation using stolen credentials, and actions on objectives by performing unauthorized actions. Detection involves monitoring for unusual patterns, while remediation includes user training and implementing advanced security measures.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes TTPs like phishing and credential theft, which are challenging to change. The use of AI and residential proxies complicates detection. No specific hashes, IPs, or domains were identified, indicating a focus on behavioral indicators and advanced detection methods. The summary highlights the need for adaptive security measures.

doc_summary: North Korea's Kimsuky group, under the Reconnaissance General Bureau, is advancing its cyber espionage capabilities by integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into its operations. South Korean security firm Genians uncovered this setup, revealing that Kimsuky is running AI offline on its own servers, using tools like Ollama, GPT4All, and Msty. These tools are configured to connect document-search capabilities to files in their possession, indicating a focus on research and knowledge acquisition. The group is not creating new AI models but is assembling existing tools to enhance its malware and data analysis capabilities. This development poses a challenge for defenders, as AI-generated content can bypass traditional detection methods. Genians' report advises correlating LNK execution, PowerShell, hidden scheduled tasks, and GitHub traffic for detection. The operation, dubbed Operation GitPower, uses GitHub repositories as command channels in an LNK-to-PowerShell infection chain, distributing encrypted AsyncRAT payloads disguised as image files. The U.S. Treasury sanctioned Kimsuky in 2023, describing it as focused on intelligence collection.
kill_chain_summary: Kimsuky's operation involves multiple stages, including reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. The group uses AI tools to enhance malware capabilities and employs GitHub as a command and control channel. Their focus is on intelligence collection, targeting government and strategic sectors.

Title: Exploitation of Atlassian Rovo Assistant for Data Exfiltration

Victim.Description: Organizations using Atlassian's Rovo assistant with Jira and Confluence.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves exploitation of vulnerabilities in Atlassian's Rovo assistant by adversaries aiming to exfiltrate data from Jira and Confluence. The adversaries leverage indirect prompt-injection and URL parameter exploitation techniques. The infrastructure includes attacker-controlled servers receiving data via crafted URLs. Victims are organizations using Rovo, with data types at risk including internal documents and API keys.
doc_summary: Atlassian's Rovo assistant was found vulnerable to data exfiltration attacks by PromptArmor and Varonis Threat Labs. PromptArmor identified an indirect prompt-injection attack allowing data collection from Jira or Confluence, while Varonis discovered the RovoBlast flaw exploiting the rovoChatPrompt URL parameter. Atlassian fixed the link flaw server-side on July 8, 2026, but the content-borne path remains unresolved. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to access data a signed-in user can reach, posing a risk to organizations using Rovo across Atlassian products. No CVE identifiers were assigned, and the issues were disclosed through Bugcrowd.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable Rovo configurations, followed by weaponization through crafting malicious content and URLs. Delivery occurs via user interactions with Rovo, leading to exploitation of vulnerabilities for unauthorized actions. Command and control is established with attacker servers, culminating in data exfiltration from Jira and Confluence. The link flaw was fixed server-side, but the content-borne path remains unresolved.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes TTPs such as indirect prompt-injection and URL parameter exploitation. No specific hash values, IP addresses, or domain names were identified. The tools and techniques used in the attack are significant, but the lack of specific indicators limits the ability to apply the Pyramid of Pain effectively. The scoring reflects the absence of concrete indicators, focusing on the TTPs employed.

Title: Exploitation of CVE-2026-8037 in Progress Kemp LoadMaster

Victim.Description: Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies and other entities using Progress Kemp LoadMaster

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a critical command injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-8037) in Progress Kemp LoadMaster appliances. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands. Active exploitation attempts have been observed from multiple countries. Federal agencies are advised to patch systems by August 10, 2026.
doc_summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a critical-severity security flaw impacting Progress Kemp LoadMaster to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-8037, is a command injection flaw with a CVSS score of 9.6, allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on the LoadMaster appliance. The flaw stems from improper handling of user-supplied input in the escape_quotes function. Active exploitation attempts have been observed, with 792 attempts from 65 unique IP addresses across 18 countries, including the United States, China, and Australia. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies are advised to apply patches by August 10, 2026, as per Binding Operational Directive 26-04. eSentire noted active exploitation efforts, though largely unsuccessful.
kill_chain_summary: The exploitation of CVE-2026-8037 represents a significant threat, allowing attackers to gain initial access through command injection. The vulnerability is actively exploited, with numerous attempts detected globally. Patching is critical to prevent unauthorized command execution on affected systems.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses from 18 countries involved in exploitation attempts. The primary TTP is the exploitation of CVE-2026-8037, a command injection vulnerability. Monitoring and patching are essential to mitigate this critical threat.

Title: UNC6671 Data Extortion Campaign Targeting Financial and Professional Services

Victim.Description: UNC6671 targets financial services, private equity, and professional services sectors in North America, Australia, and the United Kingdom.

diamond_model_summary: UNC6671 is a sophisticated data extortion group targeting financial and professional services sectors. They employ vishing and adversary-in-the-middle techniques to intercept credentials and MFA tokens, allowing access to enterprise cloud environments and SaaS applications. The group operates under multiple extortion brands and has extorted over $10.6 million in Bitcoin payments. Their infrastructure includes spoofed login portals and adversary-controlled MFA devices, highlighting the need for phishing-resistant MFA and monitoring of IdP logs.
doc_summary: UNC6671, a data extortion group, has been targeting financial services, private equity, and professional services using vishing techniques. They impersonate IT help desk staff to trick employees into providing credentials via spoofed login portals. The group uses adversary-in-the-middle infrastructure to intercept credentials and MFA tokens, allowing them to access enterprise cloud environments and SaaS applications like Microsoft 365 and Okta. UNC6671 operates under multiple extortion brands, including Redact, Pink, Helix, and Falcon, and has been linked to ShinyHunters. The group has extorted over $10.6 million in Bitcoin payments. Organizations are advised to implement phishing-resistant MFA and monitor IdP logs for suspicious activity.
kill_chain_summary: UNC6671's attack chain begins with reconnaissance to identify targets, followed by weaponization through vishing campaigns. Delivery occurs via calls to personal devices, exploiting trust to redirect victims to spoofed login portals. Installation involves registering adversary-controlled MFA devices, while command and control is achieved through captured credentials. Actions on objectives include data exfiltration from cloud environments. Detection and remediation focus on monitoring IdP logs, implementing phishing-resistant MFA, and restricting authentication to trusted networks.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for UNC6671 includes domain names like fraudulent Okta login pages and tools such as Python and PowerShell scripts. Their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) involve vishing, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, and credential theft. Detection focuses on monitoring IdP logs and call patterns, while remediation includes phishing-resistant MFA and session controls. The group's infrastructure and techniques highlight the need for robust security measures to counter their sophisticated attacks.

Title: ClickFix-Style Attack Delivers Go-Based Malware Targeting Cryptocurrency and Credentials

Victim.Description: macOS users targeted for cryptocurrency and credential theft.

diamond_model_summary: The ClickFix-style attack involves an adversary using a Go-based malware to target macOS systems, focusing on cryptocurrency theft and credential harvesting. The infrastructure is linked to Aeza Group, a Russian bulletproof hosting provider. The victim profile includes macOS users with cryptocurrency assets and stored credentials.
doc_summary: ClickFix-style attacks are being used to deliver a Go-based malware capable of stealing cryptocurrency assets, browser-stored passwords, Apple iCloud Keychain data, and cached credentials. The macOS-focused infection chain delivers a shell script that profiles the host and fetches a macOS malware payload compatible with the computer's CPU architecture. The malware payload can deplete cryptocurrency accounts, siphoning contents into accounts under the threat actor's control. The attack chain begins with pasting a ClickFix command into the Terminal app, triggering a Bash profiler/loader that collects system details and retrieves a Mach-O payload. The payload is a Go-based stealer that captures browser passwords, Apple Keychain data, and cached credentials, transmitting them to a remote server operated by the threat actor. The malware escalates privileges by prompting the victim to enter system credentials via a fake prompt. It includes a 'DRAIN' routine that checks cryptocurrency wallets and redirects funds to an attacker-controlled wallet. The server staging the malicious payloads and the C2 server link back to infrastructure belonging to Aeza Group, a Russian bulletproof hosting provider sanctioned by the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.
kill_chain_summary: The attack chain begins with a ClickFix command executed in the Terminal app, leading to the delivery of a Go-based stealer malware. The malware exploits the system to install a Mach-O payload, communicates with a C2 server, and performs actions on objectives by stealing cryptocurrency and credentials.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes the use of a Go-based stealer malware and infrastructure linked to Aeza Group. The adversary employs ClickFix commands and privilege escalation tactics, making detection challenging. The lack of specific IOCs like hashes or IPs limits the ability to disrupt the attack.

Title: Malicious npm Packages Deliver Cross-Platform Malware

Victim.Description: The campaign targets developers using npm packages and potentially Russian financial institutions.

diamond_model_summary: The adversary has launched a sophisticated supply chain attack using typo-squatting on npm packages to deliver cross-platform malware. The campaign, known as Flooding Dropper, targets developers and potentially Russian financial institutions. The adversary employs advanced techniques such as DNS TXT record-based payload delivery and uses Cloudflare Workers for command and control.
doc_summary: A cluster of nearly 800 malicious packages was published to the npm registry, targeting Windows, Mac, and Linux systems with cross-platform malware. The packages use AI-generated typo-squatting names to deliver a RAT and infostealer payload. The attack involves a downloader named WEL1DROPPER, which fetches payloads from Cloudflare Workers. If HTTPS downloads fail, DNS TXT records are used. The campaign, tracked as Flooding Dropper by Sonatype, targets Russian financial institutions and is linked to a dependency confusion campaign named Moika. The attack also involves Google Chrome extensions that turn browsers into web crawling proxies.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify popular npm packages for typo-squatting. Weaponization involves creating malicious packages with RAT and infostealer payloads. Delivery occurs through the npm registry, exploiting the require() function for execution. Installation involves downloading additional payloads, while command and control is maintained via Cloudflare Workers and DNS. The final stage involves data exfiltration and persistence establishment.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names like wel1.ru and oob-worker.cf99-9b3.workers.dev, which are critical for command and control. The use of tools like WEL1DROPPER and Sliver indicates a high level of sophistication. The adversary's TTPs include typo-squatting and supply chain attacks, making detection and remediation challenging.

doc_summary: A use-after-free vulnerability in Linux's SCTP networking code, tracked as CVE-2026-64564 and named SCTPhantom, was discovered by Tencent researchers. This flaw, existing since 2008, allows for container escape and root access on affected systems. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on August 6, 2023, after being assigned by the kernel CVE team. It affects stable kernels prior to versions 7.1.6, 6.18.42, 6.12.101, and 6.6.148, released on August 3, 2023. The flaw requires SCTP to be reachable on the target system, limiting exposure. Tencent's Zhuque Lab demonstrated the exploit on Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04, Rocky Linux 9, RHEL 9, and OpenCloudOS. The bug involves a mix-up over identity in the kernel's handling of delete requests, leading to a use-after-free condition. The patch prevents deletes aimed at the path being processed. No public exploit code was available at the time of writing, and the flaw was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Tencent credits the discovery to its Corvus AI research pipeline.
kill_chain_summary: The SCTPhantom vulnerability follows a typical exploitation path, starting with the identification of a use-after-free bug in the Linux SCTP code. Title: Exploitation of Windows Hello for Business Key for Unauthorized Access

Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable to exploitation of authentication mechanisms

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves an adversary exploiting a vulnerability in Windows Hello for Business to gain unauthorized access to Microsoft Entra ID. The adversary uses the compromised session to register devices and obtain Primary Refresh Tokens (PRTs), leveraging the ticketing behavior of Windows Hello for Business. The infrastructure involves using compromised endpoints to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID, with ROADtools being a key tool in the exploitation process. Victims are users of Windows Hello for Business with signed-in sessions, primarily in the technology sector.
doc_summary: Dirk-jan Mollema demonstrated a technique where malware in a signed-in Windows session can use the victim's Windows Hello for Business key to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. This allows attackers to establish cloud access, register devices, and obtain a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) without extracting private keys or requiring administrator privileges. The technique exploits the ticketing behavior of Windows Hello for Business, presented at DEF CON 32 in 2024. The method treats the key as a FIDO2 passkey via WebAuthn, enabling attackers to request signed assertions on another host. ROADtools can use these assertions to request tokens or open browser sessions as the victim. The token lacks a device ID claim, allowing attackers to register new devices and request PRTs. Mollema's PowerShell scripts, fido_assertion.ps1 and hellopoc.ps1, are available in the ROADtools repository. Monitoring for Windows Hello for Business sign-ins with empty device IDs is recommended for detection.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves exploiting a vulnerability in Windows Hello for Business to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID without user interaction. The adversary uses the compromised session to register devices and obtain Primary Refresh Tokens (PRTs). The exploitation stage involves using alternate authentication material, while the actions on objectives stage involves registering devices and obtaining PRTs. Detection involves monitoring for Windows Hello for Business sign-ins with empty device IDs, and remediation includes implementing monitoring for unexpected device registrations and reviewing Conditional Access policies.

doc_summary: Coinspect identified a critical vulnerability in the CryptoJS.lib.WordArray.random() function, affecting wallet apps generating recovery phrases. diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a vulnerability in Apple's iCloud Private Relay, where WebKit features such as DNS prefetching, WebAuthn Related Origin Requests, and WebTransport can expose a user's real IP address. This affects iOS, iPadOS, and macOS devices using WebKit-based browsers. The issue was discovered by researchers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk, who provided a proof-of-concept website to demonstrate the IP leak. Apple is currently investigating the report.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk disclosed a security issue with Apple's iCloud Private Relay tool, which can expose a user's real IP address. The issue is rooted in three features of Apple's WebKit: DNS prefetching, WebAuthn Related Origin Requests, and WebTransport. These features bypass the configured proxy and send traffic directly from the device, affecting iCloud Private Relay. The issue impacts iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, as well as any WebKit-based browser. A proof-of-concept website, leaks.psylo[.]app, demonstrates the IP leak. Apple is investigating the report.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves the exploitation of WebKit features to leak IP addresses, bypassing iCloud Private Relay's privacy protections. The vulnerability allows websites to configure WebAuthn in a way that reveals the user's real IP address, bypassing proxy configurations. This does not require user interaction and affects devices using WebKit-based browsers. The issue is under investigation by Apple.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes the exposure of IP addresses due to a vulnerability in WebKit features. The proof-of-concept website leaks.psylo[.]app demonstrates the IP leak. No specific hashes, domains, or tools were identified beyond the domain used for testing. The incident highlights the need for monitoring WebKit traffic and applying patches once available.

Title: Factory-Shipped Backdoor in Zbtlink Routers: ENDLESSDOORS

Victim.Description: Victims are users of Zbtlink routers with affected firmware versions.
Victim.Geography: Primarily China, potentially global due to distribution of affected routers.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a factory-shipped backdoor in Zbtlink routers, codenamed ENDLESSDOORS. The adversary uses this backdoor to establish command-and-control channels with compromised routers. The capability includes the use of the rctl tool for remote control, while the infrastructure involves C2 servers that the backdoor attempts to contact. Victims are users of affected Zbtlink routers, primarily in the telecommunications sector.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified a factory-shipped backdoor in at least 20 Chinese router models from Zbtlink. The backdoor, named ENDLESSDOORS, is present in all 21 firmware images available from Zbtlink over the past two years. It masquerades as a Linux kernel thread but operates as a userland process with root privileges, attempting to connect to Chinese command-and-control infrastructure every 35 seconds. The backdoor uses a tool called rctl, uploaded to GitHub in 2015, which allows remote control via port 7000. The implant can execute shell commands or spawn a reverse bash shell. The lack of authentication in the protocol allows attackers to hijack communications and gain root access. VulnCheck's analysis of the Zbtlink AX3000 model revealed the use of a customized rctl version. Affected firmware versions have been removed from Zbtlink's website, and users are advised to check for specific files and block egress points.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain for this incident involves the installation of a backdoor in Zbtlink router firmware, which is pre-installed and activated at boot. The command-and-control stage involves the backdoor establishing a connection with a remote server using the rctl tool. Actions on objectives include the execution of shell commands and spawning of a reverse shell, allowing the adversary to control the compromised routers.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names such as rbdg4nzqadui.wikaba.com, which are used for command-and-control communication. Network host artifacts include files like /usr/sbin/kworker and /etc/init.d/skworker, which are indicative of the backdoor's presence. The use of the rctl tool and the ENDLESSDOORS malware family are key indicators of compromise.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves vulnerabilities in agent infrastructures from AWS, Google, and Vercel, allowing unauthorized tool execution. The infrastructure includes agent development kits and SDKs, with a high impact severity on the technology sector.
doc_summary: Security flaws were identified in agent infrastructures from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google, and Vercel, allowing untrusted instructions to reach agent tools without proper authorization. The affected products include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore's InvokeHarness API, Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, and Vercel AI SDK harness packages. AWS assigned CVE-2026-18830 to the issue, with a CVSS score of 8.6, and implemented server-side validation. Google's flaw, CVE-2026-18236, had a CVSS score of 9.3, and Vercel's issues were tracked as CVE-2026-64650 and CVE-2026-64651, both with a CVSS score of 6.3. The vulnerabilities allowed unauthorized tool execution by bypassing model-level checks. The flaws were presented by Stealth co-founders at Black Hat USA 2026.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves exploiting authorization bypass vulnerabilities in agent infrastructures, leading to unauthorized tool execution. The exploitation stage is marked by the use of valid accounts to bypass checks, while actions on objectives involve executing unauthorized commands. Detection and remediation focus on monitoring tool execution and implementing robust authorization mechanisms.

Title: SQL Injection Exploit in Oracle Database Leads to SYSTEM-Level Compromise

Victim.Description: An organization with a vulnerable Oracle database exposed to SQL injection.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to unvalidated input and excessive privileges.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves an unknown adversary exploiting a SQL injection vulnerability in an Oracle database. The adversary's capability includes executing Java code within the database, leveraging the askhunt toolkit. The infrastructure targeted includes the Oracle database and underlying Windows server. The victim is an organization with a vulnerable public-facing web application.
doc_summary: Attackers exploited a SQL injection flaw in a public-facing web application to compromise an Oracle database. They installed a post-exploitation toolkit without writing an executable to disk by feeding Java source code to the database, which Oracle compiled into stored schema objects. Huntress investigated the incident after credential-theft detections on July 27, 2026, tracing it to SYSTEM-level code execution on a Windows server. The flaw was in an autocomplete search field passing unvalidated input over a JDBC connection. The compromised account had enough privilege to create Java objects. No Oracle patch exists for the application flaw or account privilege. The toolkit, identified by object names beginning with Khunt, used Java classes compiled into database schema objects. The attackers used cmd.exe, PowerShell, and reg.exe to manipulate registry hives and task lists. The malicious requests were traced to IP 178.162.151.229. The fix involves parameterized queries, input validation, and least privilege principles.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with the exploitation of a SQL injection vulnerability, allowing the adversary to execute Java code within the Oracle database. This led to the installation of a post-exploitation toolkit, enabling SYSTEM-level command execution on the underlying Windows server. The attackers collected registry hives and task lists, indicating potential data exfiltration objectives.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and tools used by the adversary. The IP address 178.162.151.229 was associated with the malicious requests. Tools such as cmd.exe, PowerShell, and reg.exe were used for command execution and data collection. These indicators can aid in detecting and responding to similar threats.
